subject: HSS
title: U.S. History and Geography: Growth and Conflict
description: Grade 8 United States history from the ideas behind the American Revolution through the Constitution, the early Republic, regional divergence, westward expansion, the Civil War, Reconstruction and the rise of industrial America. Students read primary sources every week (founding documents, speeches, letters, photographs and maps), practice historical thinking skills such as sourcing and corroboration, and write evidence-based arguments.
framework: California History-Social Science Content Standards (Grade 8); 2016 California History-Social Science Framework

standards.8.1: Understand the major events preceding the founding of the nation and their significance to American constitutional democracy.
standards.8.1.1: Describe how the moral and political ideas of the Great Awakening related to revolutionary fervor.
standards.8.1.2: Analyze the philosophy of government in the Declaration of Independence, emphasizing government as a means of securing individual rights.
standards.8.1.3: Analyze how the American Revolution affected other nations, especially France.
standards.8.1.4: Describe the nation's blend of civic republicanism, classical liberal principles, and English parliamentary traditions.
standards.8.2: Analyze the political principles underlying the U.S. Constitution and compare enumerated and implied powers.
standards.8.2.1: Discuss the significance of the Magna Carta, the English Bill of Rights, and the Mayflower Compact.
standards.8.2.2: Analyze the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution and how well each implemented the ideals of the Declaration.
standards.8.2.3: Evaluate major debates at the Constitutional Convention (shared power, state-federal power, slavery, individual rights, American Indian nations) and their resolutions.
standards.8.2.4: Describe the philosophy of the Federalist Papers and the roles of Madison, Washington, Sherman, Morris and Wilson in writing and ratifying the Constitution.
standards.8.2.5: Understand Jefferson's Statute for Religious Freedom as a forerunner of the First Amendment and views on separation of church and state.
standards.8.2.6: Enumerate the powers of government in the Constitution and the fundamental liberties ensured by the Bill of Rights.
standards.8.2.7: Describe federalism, separation of powers, checks and balances, majority rule, and how constitutionalism preserves individual rights.
standards.8.3: Understand the foundation of the American political system and the ways citizens participate in it.
standards.8.3.1: Analyze principles codified in state constitutions of 1777-1781.
standards.8.3.2: Explain how the Land Ordinance of 1785 and Northwest Ordinance of 1787 transferred federal lands to private holdings, townships and states.
standards.8.3.3: Enumerate the advantages of a common market among the states protected by the Constitution.
standards.8.3.4: Understand how conflicts between Jefferson and Hamilton led to two political parties.
standards.8.3.5: Know the significance of domestic resistance movements (Shays' Rebellion, Whiskey Rebellion) and the government's response.
standards.8.3.6: Describe the law-making process and how citizens participate in and influence government.
standards.8.3.7: Understand the functions and responsibilities of a free press.
standards.8.4: Analyze the aspirations and ideals of the people of the new nation.
standards.8.4.1: Describe the country's landscapes, political divisions and territorial expansion under the first four presidents.
standards.8.4.2: Explain the policy significance of famous speeches (Washington's Farewell Address, Jefferson's 1801 Inaugural, J. Q. Adams's 1821 address).
standards.8.4.3: Analyze the rise of capitalism and related conflicts (the National Bank, early Supreme Court decisions on contracts).
standards.8.4.4: Discuss daily life, art, music and literature of early national America (Washington Irving, James Fenimore Cooper).
standards.8.5: Analyze U.S. foreign policy in the early Republic.
standards.8.5.1: Understand the causes, consequences, major battles and leaders of the War of 1812.
standards.8.5.2: Know changing U.S. boundaries and relations with Mexico, Canada and Europe, including the Monroe Doctrine.
standards.8.5.3: Outline major treaties with American Indian nations under the first four presidents and their outcomes.
standards.8.6: Analyze the divergent paths of the American people from 1800 to the mid-1800s, with emphasis on the Northeast.
standards.8.6.1: Discuss the influence of industrialization and technology on the Northeast and human modification of the landscape.
standards.8.6.2: Outline obstacles and factors in building roads, canals and railroads (Henry Clay's American System).
standards.8.6.3: List reasons for immigration from Northern Europe and describe the growth of cities (Irish Famine).
standards.8.6.4: Study the lives of free Black Americans in the North who founded schools and churches.
standards.8.6.5: Trace the development of American education, including Horace Mann's campaign for free public schools.
standards.8.6.6: Examine the women's rights movement (Stanton, Fuller, Mott, Anthony).
standards.8.6.7: Identify themes in American art, transcendentalism and individualism (Emerson, Thoreau, Melville, Alcott, Hawthorne, Longfellow).
standards.8.7: Analyze the divergent paths of the American people in the South from 1800 to the mid-1800s.
standards.8.7.1: Describe the South's agrarian economy, cotton-producing states, and the significance of cotton and the cotton gin.
standards.8.7.2: Trace the origins and development of slavery, its effects, and strategies to overturn or preserve it (Nat Turner, Denmark Vesey).
standards.8.7.3: Examine white Southern society and how the physical environment influenced conditions before the Civil War.
standards.8.7.4: Compare the lives and opportunities of free Black people in the North and in the South.
standards.8.8: Analyze the divergent paths of the American people in the West from 1800 to the mid-1800s.
standards.8.8.1: Discuss Andrew Jackson's election, Jacksonian democracy, and his actions (spoils system, Bank veto, Indian removal).
standards.8.8.2: Describe westward expansion and Manifest Destiny (Lewis and Clark, Trail of Tears, Great Plains settlement, territorial acquisitions).
standards.8.8.3: Describe the role of pioneer women and the new status western women achieved.
standards.8.8.4: Examine the importance of the great rivers and struggles over water rights.
standards.8.8.5: Discuss Mexican settlements, cultural traditions, attitudes toward slavery, land-grant system and economies.
standards.8.8.6: Describe the Texas War for Independence and the Mexican-American War and their effects, including on Mexican Americans today.
standards.8.9: Analyze the early and steady attempts to abolish slavery and realize the ideals of the Declaration of Independence.
standards.8.9.1: Describe leaders of the abolition movement (Douglass, Garrison, Tubman, John Brown, Weld, J. Q. Adams).
standards.8.9.2: Discuss the abolition of slavery in early state constitutions.
standards.8.9.3: Describe the significance of the Northwest Ordinance for education and banning slavery north of the Ohio River.
standards.8.9.4: Discuss the slavery issue raised by Texas annexation and California's admission as a free state in the Compromise of 1850.
standards.8.9.5: Analyze states' rights doctrine, the Missouri Compromise, Wilmot Proviso, Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act, Dred Scott decision and Lincoln-Douglas debates.
standards.8.9.6: Describe the lives of free Black people and the laws that limited their freedom and opportunities.
standards.8.10: Analyze the multiple causes, key events, and complex consequences of the Civil War.
standards.8.10.1: Compare interpretations of state and federal authority in the writings of Daniel Webster and John C. Calhoun.
standards.8.10.2: Trace boundaries and geographic and economic differences between North and South.
standards.8.10.3: Identify constitutional issues posed by nullification and secession.
standards.8.10.4: Discuss Lincoln's presidency and writings (House Divided, Gettysburg Address, Emancipation Proclamation, inaugural addresses).
standards.8.10.5: Study leaders and soldiers on both sides, including Black soldiers and regiments.
standards.8.10.6: Describe major battles, geographic advantages, technology, and Lee's surrender at Appomattox.
standards.8.10.7: Explain how the war affected combatants, civilians, the environment and future warfare.
standards.8.11: Analyze the character and lasting consequences of Reconstruction.
standards.8.11.1: List the original aims of Reconstruction and its effects on political and social structures.
standards.8.11.2: Identify push-pull factors in the movement of freedpeople to Northern cities and the West (Buffalo Soldiers).
standards.8.11.3: Understand the Freedmen's Bureau and restrictions on freedpeople, including segregation and Jim Crow laws.
standards.8.11.4: Trace the rise of the Ku Klux Klan and its effects.
standards.8.11.5: Understand the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments and their connection to Reconstruction.
standards.8.12: Analyze the transformation of the American economy and changing social and political conditions in response to the Industrial Revolution.
standards.8.12.1: Trace patterns of agricultural and industrial development related to climate, resources, markets and trade.
standards.8.12.2: Identify reasons for federal Indian policy and the wars with American Indians and their link to development.
standards.8.12.3: Explain how governments encouraged business expansion through tariffs, banking, land grants and subsidies.
standards.8.12.4: Discuss entrepreneurs, industrialists and bankers (Carnegie, Rockefeller, Leland Stanford).
standards.8.12.5: Examine the effects of urbanization, renewed immigration and industrialization, including the conservation movement.
standards.8.12.6: Discuss child labor, working conditions, laissez-faire policy and the labor movement (Samuel Gompers).
standards.8.12.7: Identify new sources of immigration, immigrant contributions, assimilation, and nativism.
standards.8.12.8: Identify the characteristics and impact of Grangerism and Populism.
standards.8.12.9: Name significant inventors and inventions (Edison, Bell, the Wright brothers) and how they improved life.

units.title: Roots of Revolution and the Declaration
units.big_idea: Enlightenment and English traditions inspired colonists to claim natural rights and declare independence.

units.title: Creating the Constitution
units.big_idea: The framers replaced a weak confederation with a Constitution balancing power, rights and compromise, including compromises over slavery.

units.title: Launching the New Nation
units.big_idea: Early leaders turned the Constitution into a working government, sparking party conflict and debates about national identity.

units.title: Foreign Policy and the Industrializing Northeast
units.big_idea: The young nation asserted itself abroad while the Northeast industrialized and reformers pushed for change.

units.title: The South and Slavery
units.big_idea: Cotton made slavery central to the Southern economy, while enslaved people resisted in many ways.

units.title: Jacksonian Democracy and Westward Expansion
units.big_idea: Expanding democracy and Manifest Destiny drove growth that came at great cost to American Indians and Mexico.

units.title: Abolition and the Road to Civil War
units.big_idea: Reform movements and failed compromises over slavery's expansion split the nation.

units.title: The Civil War
units.big_idea: The war to preserve the Union became a war to end slavery, transforming the nation.

units.title: Reconstruction
units.big_idea: Reconstruction amendments expanded freedom, but violence and Jim Crow laws rolled back many gains.

units.title: Industrial America
units.big_idea: Industry, railroads and immigration transformed the economy and society, prompting labor and farmer movements.

units.title: Year in Review
units.big_idea: The struggle to realize the ideals of the Declaration connects every era studied this year.

weeks.topic: Foundations: English rights and Enlightenment ideas
objectives: Explain how the Magna Carta, English Bill of Rights and Mayflower Compact shaped colonial ideas
Identify Enlightenment ideas of Locke and Montesquieu

days.title: Course launch & historical thinking
days.work: Set up an interactive notebook and timeline (1750–1900); practice sourcing a document by asking who, when, why and how reliable.

days.title: Magna Carta & English Bill of Rights
days.work: Read excerpts of the Magna Carta (1215) and English Bill of Rights (1689); list rights each limited the king's power over.

days.title: Mayflower Compact
days.work: Read the full Mayflower Compact (1620) and annotate examples of self-government and consent.

days.title: Enlightenment thinkers
days.work: Read short excerpts from Locke's Second Treatise and Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws; make a chart linking each idea to American government.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph answering 'Where did American ideas about rights come from?' citing two documents.

weeks.assessment: Document-based paragraph scored for claim and evidence.

weeks.topic: The Great Awakening and the road to revolution
objectives: Connect the Great Awakening to questioning authority
Sequence events from the French and Indian War to Lexington and Concord

days.title: Great Awakening
days.work: Read a short excerpt from a George Whitefield or Jonathan Edwards sermon and discuss how revival ideas encouraged questioning authority.

days.title: Taxes and protest
days.work: Create a cause-and-effect chain from the French and Indian War debt to the Stamp Act, Townshend Acts and boycotts.

days.title: Boston Massacre sources
days.work: Compare Paul Revere's engraving with Captain Preston's account; identify point of view and propaganda.

days.title: Lexington and Concord
days.work: Read eyewitness depositions from April 19, 1775 and decide who fired first using evidence.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Timeline quiz on 1754–1775 and a short sourcing response.

weeks.assessment: Sourcing response on the Boston Massacre and timeline quiz.

weeks.topic: The Declaration of Independence and the Revolution
objectives: Analyze the philosophy of government in the Declaration
Explain how the Revolution was won and its effect on France and other nations

days.title: Common Sense
days.work: Read excerpts from Thomas Paine's Common Sense and identify his three strongest arguments for independence.

days.title: The Declaration
days.work: Close-read the preamble of the Declaration; paraphrase each key phrase and list 5 grievances against the king.

days.title: Winning the war
days.work: Map key battles (Saratoga, Valley Forge, Yorktown) and explain the role of French alliance and of Black and women patriots such as James Armistead and Mercy Otis Warren.

days.title: Global impact
days.work: Compare the Declaration with the French Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789) in a Venn diagram.

days.title: Unit 1 test
days.work: Unit test and a short essay on how the Declaration defines the purpose of government.

objectives: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the Articles
Explain the importance of the Land Ordinance and Northwest Ordinance

days.title: State constitutions
days.work: Compare excerpts of the 1776 Virginia Declaration of Rights and 1780 Massachusetts Constitution; list common principles.

days.title: Articles of Confederation
days.work: Read selected articles and sort features into strengths and weaknesses.

days.title: Land ordinances
days.work: Draw a township grid using the Land Ordinance of 1785 and read the Northwest Ordinance's provisions on education and slavery.

days.title: Shays' Rebellion
days.work: Read letters reacting to Shays' Rebellion (Washington, Jefferson) and explain why leaders called for a new constitution.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz plus a paragraph: 'Were the Articles a failure?'

objectives: Evaluate the major debates and compromises at the Convention
Describe the roles of key delegates

days.title: Delegates
days.work: Create profile cards for Madison, Washington, Franklin, Sherman, Morris and Wilson.

days.title: Representation debate
days.work: Role-play the Virginia vs New Jersey Plan debate and write the Great Compromise in your own words.

days.title: Slavery and the Constitution
days.work: Analyze the Three-Fifths Clause, slave trade clause and fugitive slave clause; discuss how they contradicted the Declaration.

days.title: Other debates
days.work: Examine debates on the executive, the commerce clause and the status of American Indian nations.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on compromises and their resolutions.

weeks.topic: Ratification and the Bill of Rights
objectives: Compare Federalist and Anti-Federalist arguments
Explain the freedoms protected in the Bill of Rights

days.title: Federalists vs Anti-Federalists
days.work: Read excerpts of Federalist No. 10 and an Anti-Federalist essay (Brutus No. 1); chart main arguments.

days.title: Federalist No. 51
days.work: Analyze 'If men were angels' and explain checks and balances.

days.title: Religious freedom
days.work: Read Jefferson's Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom and connect it to the First Amendment.

days.title: Bill of Rights
days.work: Illustrate each of the first 10 amendments with a modern scenario.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Bill of Rights scenario quiz.

weeks.assessment: Scenario quiz on the Bill of Rights.

objectives: Explain federalism, separation of powers and checks and balances
Describe how a bill becomes law and how citizens participate

days.title: Structure of the Constitution
days.work: Scavenger hunt through Articles I–VII to locate powers of each branch.

days.title: Checks & balances
days.work: Create a diagram of checks between branches with real examples (veto, judicial review).

days.title: Federalism
days.work: Sort powers into federal, state and shared; discuss enumerated vs implied powers.

days.title: How a bill becomes law & the press
days.work: Trace a current bill on congress.gov; compare two news articles on it to evaluate the role of a free press.

days.title: Unit 2 test
days.work: Unit test on the Constitution.

weeks.topic: Washington's presidency and the first parties
objectives: Explain Hamilton's financial plan and Jefferson's opposition
Analyze Washington's Farewell Address

days.title: Washington's precedents
days.work: List precedents Washington set (cabinet, two terms, 'Mr. President') and their lasting effects.

days.title: Hamilton vs Jefferson
days.work: Debate the National Bank and the assumption of state debts; create a T-chart of the two visions.

days.title: Whiskey Rebellion
days.work: Compare the federal response to the Whiskey Rebellion with Shays' Rebellion.

days.title: Farewell Address
days.work: Read excerpts and identify Washington's warnings about parties and foreign alliances.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on the Washington years and party formation.

weeks.topic: Adams, Jefferson and the Louisiana Purchase
objectives: Analyze the Alien and Sedition Acts and the election of 1800
Explain the significance of the Louisiana Purchase and Lewis and Clark

days.title: Adams and the Alien and Sedition Acts
days.work: Read the Sedition Act and argue whether it violated the First Amendment.

days.title: Jefferson's Inaugural
days.work: Read Jefferson's 1801 Inaugural Address excerpt: 'We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.'

days.title: Marbury v. Madison
days.work: Summarize the case and explain judicial review.

days.title: Louisiana Purchase & Lewis and Clark
days.work: Map the purchase and route; read journal entries and Sacagawea's role.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Map quiz and short answer.

weeks.assessment: Map quiz on 1803 territories and expedition route.

weeks.topic: Life, economy and culture in the early Republic
objectives: Describe daily life, art and literature of early America
Outline early treaties with American Indian nations
materials: 'Rip Van Winkle' by Washington Irving (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Early capitalism
days.work: Examine McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden and how they strengthened national markets.

days.title: Treaties with American Indian nations
days.work: Analyze the Treaty of Greenville (1795) and compare outcomes for Native nations.

days.title: American literature
days.work: Read 'Rip Van Winkle' and discuss what it says about the new nation.

days.title: Art and music
days.work: Analyze Gilbert Stuart and Charles Willson Peale portraits and early American songs.

days.title: Unit 3 test
days.work: Unit test on the early Republic.

weeks.topic: The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine
objectives: Explain the causes and outcomes of the War of 1812
Analyze the Monroe Doctrine

days.title: Causes
days.work: Read about impressment and Tecumseh's confederacy; chart causes of the war.

days.title: Major battles
days.work: Map major battles (Washington burned, Fort McHenry, New Orleans).

days.title: Star-Spangled Banner
days.work: Read Francis Scott Key's full poem and explain its context.

days.title: Monroe Doctrine
days.work: Read the key passage of the Monroe Doctrine and explain its message to Europe.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on the War of 1812 and foreign policy.

objectives: Explain how factories, canals and railroads transformed the Northeast
Describe immigration and city growth

days.title: Factories
days.work: Read letters from Lowell mill workers (Harriet Robinson) and describe working conditions.

days.title: Transportation revolution
days.work: Map the Erie Canal and National Road; explain Clay's American System.

days.title: Inventions
days.work: Make a chart of inventions (cotton gin, steamboat, telegraph, steel plow) and effects.

days.title: Immigration
days.work: Analyze Irish and German immigration data and a nativist cartoon.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on industrial growth in the Northeast.

objectives: Describe reform movements in education and women's rights
Identify American literary themes of the period

days.title: Free Black communities
days.work: Read about Richard Allen and the AME Church and free Black schools in the North.

days.title: Education reform
days.work: Read Horace Mann's arguments for public schools.

days.title: Women's rights
days.work: Compare the Declaration of Sentiments (1848) with the Declaration of Independence.

days.title: Transcendentalism
days.work: Read excerpts from Thoreau's Walden and Emerson's 'Self-Reliance'; discuss individualism.

days.title: Unit 4 test
days.work: Unit test on foreign policy and the Northeast.

objectives: Explain how the cotton gin expanded slavery
Describe the geography and social structure of the South
materials: maps of cotton production and enslaved population 1820 vs 1860

days.title: Geography of the South
days.work: Label cotton-producing states, major rivers and port cities on a blank map; explain how climate and soil favored cotton.

days.title: The cotton gin
days.work: Graph cotton production and the enslaved population from 1790 to 1860 and write a paragraph explaining the relationship to Whitney's 1793 gin.

days.title: Southern society
days.work: Build a social pyramid of the South (planters, yeoman farmers, poor whites, free Black people, enslaved people) using census statistics.

days.title: A one-crop economy
days.work: Trace a bale of cotton from a Mississippi plantation to a Lowell or Manchester mill and explain the South's dependence on Northern and British markets.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on the Southern economy plus a short response comparing Northern and Southern economies.

objectives: Describe life under slavery using first-person sources
Analyze forms of resistance from everyday acts to rebellion
materials: WPA Slave Narratives excerpts (Library of Congress)

days.title: Narratives of slavery
days.work: Read two WPA Slave Narrative interviews and a chapter excerpt from Harriet Jacobs's 'Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl'; note family, labor and punishment details.

days.title: Resistance and rebellion
days.work: Read excerpts from 'The Confessions of Nat Turner' (1831) and accounts of Denmark Vesey's plan; list Southern legal responses.

days.title: Culture and spirituals
days.work: Listen to 'Wade in the Water' and 'Follow the Drinking Gourd' and analyze possible double meanings in the lyrics.

days.title: Free Black people, North and South
days.work: Compare primary sources on free Black communities in Philadelphia and New Orleans in a T-chart of rights and restrictions.

days.title: Unit 5 test
days.work: Unit test on the South and slavery, including a document-based short answer.

objectives: Analyze Jackson's presidency and the expansion of suffrage
Explain the Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears

days.title: Jackson's rise
days.work: Compare voter-turnout data from 1824 and 1828 and explain how the end of property requirements expanded white male suffrage.

days.title: The Bank War
days.work: Read an excerpt from Jackson's 1832 veto message and summarize his argument against the Second Bank.

days.title: Indian Removal debate
days.work: Compare the Cherokee Memorial to Congress with Jackson's 1830 message on removal using a sourcing chart.

days.title: Trail of Tears
days.work: Map the removal routes of the Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw and Seminole and read a soldier's eyewitness account (Private John Burnett).

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a document-based paragraph: 'Was Indian Removal consistent with the Constitution?' citing Worcester v. Georgia.

weeks.topic: Manifest Destiny and the trails west
objectives: Explain the idea of Manifest Destiny and who it affected
Describe the experiences of pioneers including women

days.title: Manifest Destiny
days.work: Analyze John Gast's 'American Progress' painting and John O'Sullivan's 1845 essay; list who is shown and who is missing.

days.title: Trails west
days.work: Map the Oregon, California, Mormon and Santa Fe trails and calculate travel times at 15 miles per day.

days.title: Pioneer women
days.work: Read diary excerpts from women on the Oregon Trail and a short biography of Annie Bidwell; explain why Wyoming granted women suffrage in 1869.

days.title: Rivers and water
days.work: Examine why the Mississippi, Missouri and Colorado rivers mattered and read about early Western water-rights conflicts.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on westward expansion plus a one-paragraph analysis of Gast's painting.

weeks.topic: Mexican California and Texas independence; semester review
objectives: Describe Mexican settlements, ranchos and the land-grant system
Explain the Texas War for Independence
Review semester 1
materials: Calisphere images of ranchos and Californios

days.title: Mexican California
days.work: Use Calisphere photographs and diseños (land-grant maps) to describe rancho life, the economy of hides and tallow and Mexico's 1829 abolition of slavery.

days.title: Texas Revolution
days.work: Compare a Texan account and a Mexican account (José Enrique de la Peña) of the Alamo and identify each perspective.

days.title: Semester review A
days.work: Review Units 1–3 with a timeline sort and practice document questions.

days.title: Semester review B
days.work: Review Units 4–6 with a vocabulary matching game and a practice DBQ outline.

days.title: Semester 1 exam
days.work: Cumulative semester exam with multiple-choice and document-based items.

weeks.topic: The Mexican-American War and the Gold Rush
objectives: Explain causes and outcomes of the Mexican-American War
Describe the Gold Rush and its effects on Californians

days.title: Causes of war
days.work: Compare President Polk's 1846 war message with Lincoln's 'spot resolutions' and decide whose claim is better supported.

days.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
days.work: Read Articles 8 and 9 and evaluate whether promises of property and citizenship to Mexican residents were kept.

days.title: The Gold Rush
days.work: Read a forty-niner's letter home and examine Calisphere photos; chart impacts on Native Californians, Californios and Chinese miners.

days.title: Legacy today
days.work: Read a short article on the war's effects on Mexican Americans today and write a reflection connecting past and present.

days.title: Unit 6 test
days.work: Unit test on Jacksonian democracy and westward expansion.

objectives: Describe abolitionist leaders and strategies
Explain abolition in early state constitutions and the Northwest Ordinance

days.title: Early abolition
days.work: Read Pennsylvania's 1780 Gradual Abolition Act and the Northwest Ordinance's Article 6; map Northern states' abolition dates.

days.title: Garrison and Douglass
days.work: Read Garrison's 'To the Public' (1831) and Douglass's 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' (1852); compare tone and strategy.

days.title: Underground Railroad
days.work: Map major routes and read about Harriet Tubman's missions and William Still's records.

days.title: Free Black lives and laws
days.work: Read about Northern Black laws (e.g., Ohio's 1804 law) and the achievements of leaders such as James Forten.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on abolitionists and their strategies.

objectives: Analyze the Missouri Compromise, Wilmot Proviso and Compromise of 1850
Explain why California's admission as a free state mattered
materials: maps of free and slave states in 1820 and 1850

days.title: Missouri Compromise
days.work: Color a map showing the 36°30' line and explain Henry Clay's role in balancing free and slave states.

days.title: Wilmot Proviso
days.work: Read the one-sentence Wilmot Proviso (1846) and explain why it divided Congress along sectional rather than party lines.

days.title: Compromise of 1850
days.work: Chart each part of the Compromise of 1850 (including California statehood) and score which side gained more.

days.title: Fugitive Slave Act
days.work: Read accounts of the Anthony Burns case in Boston and explain how the act radicalized Northerners.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on compromises and a map-labeling task.

weeks.topic: Bleeding Kansas, Dred Scott and the rise of Lincoln
objectives: Explain the Kansas-Nebraska Act and the Dred Scott decision
Analyze the Lincoln-Douglas debates

days.title: Kansas-Nebraska Act
days.work: Map the act and explain how popular sovereignty undid the Missouri Compromise and led to violence in Kansas.

days.title: Dred Scott
days.work: Read excerpts of Chief Justice Taney's opinion and list the decision's three main holdings and their effects.

days.title: A House Divided
days.work: Close-read Lincoln's 'House Divided' speech and explain its central metaphor in your own words.

days.title: Lincoln-Douglas debates
days.work: Compare Lincoln's and Douglas's positions on slavery's expansion using debate excerpts in a T-chart.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a DBQ paragraph: 'Was the Civil War inevitable by 1858?'

objectives: Compare Webster and Calhoun on state vs federal authority
Explain why Southern states seceded after 1860
materials: Webster's Second Reply to Hayne excerpt
South Carolina Declaration of the Causes of Secession (1860)
